key_facts: A **non-immune phototoxic** reaction: plant **furocoumarins** (psoralens) on the skin plus **UVA** light.
Anyone can be affected with enough sap and sun; no previous sensitisation is needed.
Burning redness and **blisters** appear about **24 h** after exposure and peak at **48–72 h**, in **streaks, drips or hand-prints**.
**Hyperpigmentation** follows and can last months to years; it is often why people present.
Manage like a superficial burn: wash sap off, keep out of sun for 48 h, short topical steroid, strict sun protection. Think **safeguarding** with odd marks in children.

sections.title: Overview
blocks: Phytophotodermatitis is a **phototoxic** skin reaction that happens when light-sensitising chemicals in some plants (**furocoumarins**, also called psoralens) get on the skin and are then exposed to **ultraviolet A (UVA)**. It is not an allergy: the sap and light damage the skin directly, so it can happen to anyone at first exposure.

ul: The burn has **bizarre, geometric shapes** (streaks, drips, splashes, finger- and hand-prints) that trace where the juice or sap touched.
It heals with **brown pigmentation** that can persist for months.
Classic UK sources: **giant hogweed**, wild parsnip and rue (strimming, walking), and **limes** (cocktails and cooking on holiday).
**Berloque dermatitis** is a variant from bergamot-containing perfume on the neck.

sub: Any age, sex or skin type; incidence is unknown because mild cases are not reported.
Mostly **summer** and sunny holidays, when people handle plants or citrus outdoors.
Gardeners, farm and grounds workers, bartenders and chefs (limes), children playing outdoors, hikers.
Fair skin may burn more readily, while darker skin shows more marked and longer-lasting pigmentation.

sections.title: Aetiology: causes and risk factors
blocks: Two things are needed: a **furocoumarin on the skin** and enough **UVA**. Moisture (sweat, water) and heat increase absorption and the reaction.

head: Family
Examples
rows: **Giant hogweed**, cow parsley, wild and cultivated **parsnip**, celery, carrot, fennel, dill, parsley
**Lime**, lemon, bergamot orange, bitter orange, grapefruit, **rue**
Some St John's wort and other garden plants

ul: **Activities**: strimming or mowing weeds, clearing riverbanks, picking wild plants, squeezing limes or making drinks in the sun.
**Berloque dermatitis**: perfume containing bergamot oil (5-methoxypsoralen) applied to the neck, then sun.
**"It must be an allergy"**: no; phototoxicity needs no sensitisation and anyone can react.
**"It was a sunburn"**: plain sunburn is uniform over exposed skin; the streaks and drips point to a plant or citrus.
**"The marks are bruises or scars"**: they are pigment and fade slowly without scarring.

mech.t: Furocoumarins in plant sap or citrus juice penetrate the epidermis. **UVA (320–400 nm, peak effect around 335 nm)** activates them; a cloudy day still delivers enough UVA.
mech.caption: Step 1: furocoumarin-rich sap (e.g. hogweed) on skin, then UVA exposure.

mech.k: Phototoxic damage to DNA and membranes
mech.t: Activated psoralens act in two ways: **type I** reactions bind directly to **DNA**, forming cross-links between strands; **type II** reactions generate reactive oxygen species that damage cell membranes. No immune memory is involved.
mech.caption: Step 2: UVA-activated psoralen molecules slot between DNA strands and cross-link them.

mech.t: Damaged keratinocytes die ("sunburn cells"), with dermal oedema and inflammation. Severe damage separates the epidermis, producing **vesicles and bullae** after about 24 h, peaking at 48–72 h.
mech.caption: Step 3: necrotic keratinocytes and an intraepidermal blister above an inflamed dermis.

mech.t: Psoralen–UVA stimulates **melanocytes** to make more melanin and melanin drops into the dermis where **melanophages** hold it, so brown or grey-brown pigment appears 1–2 weeks later and lasts months.
mech.caption: Step 4: active melanocytes and pigment-laden melanophages in the upper dermis cause the long-lasting brown marks.

fig.caption: The shape gives it away: drips, streaks and hand-prints that follow where juice or sap touched the skin.
fig.alt: Limbs and hand with streaky and hand-print burns

histo: Acute: necrotic keratinocytes, spongiosis, intraepidermal or subepidermal **vesicles**, dermal oedema and a mild perivascular infiltrate (like an acute sunburn).
Late: **pigment incontinence** with melanophages in the upper dermis and increased basal melanin.
Biopsy is rarely needed; history and shape are diagnostic.

ul: **Burning or stinging pain** more than itch, starting about 24 h after sun exposure.
Usually no systemic symptoms, except with extensive hogweed burns.
Later, **brown marks** with no memory of the inflammatory phase: often the presenting complaint.

lesions.name: Streaky erythema
lesions.t: Sharply outlined **linear streaks** of redness and oedema where sap brushed the skin.

lesions.name: Vesicles and bullae
lesions.t: Tense blisters, sometimes large, resembling a partial-thickness burn.

lesions.name: Drips and hand-prints
lesions.t: Drip, splash and finger-print shapes from citrus juice.

lesions.name: Hyperpigmentation
lesions.t: Brown to grey-brown streaks that persist for months after the burn settles.

ul: **Exposed skin** that touched the plant or juice: hands, forearms, legs and ankles (strimming), around the mouth and chin (citrus), neck (perfume).
Shapes follow contact, **not** the whole sun-exposed area (unlike drug photosensitivity).

figs.caption: Linear redness and blisters after strimming.
Streaks where juice brushed the skin: an outside cause.

variants.name: Lime ("margarita") dermatitis
variants.t: Drips and hand-prints on hands, wrists, face and chest after squeezing limes in the sun.

variants.name: Giant hogweed burn
variants.t: Severe blistering on arms and legs after contact with sap on riverbanks and verges; can need burns care.

variants.name: Bullous phytophotodermatitis
variants.t: Large blisters, usually on the lower legs and ankles.

variants.name: Pigmentation-only presentation
variants.t: Streaky brown marks without remembered redness.

variants.name: Berloque dermatitis
variants.t: Pendant-shaped streaks on the neck from bergamot perfume plus sun.

sub: Hand-print or splash patterns can look like **bruising or non-accidental injury**; take a careful plant and sun history and follow safeguarding procedures if the story does not fit.
Redness may be subtle; the **hyperpigmentation** is often marked and lasts longer.

figs.caption: Residual pigmentation for months; atypical patterns in children need a careful history.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: Diagnosis is **clinical**, from the **bizarre shape** plus an **exposure history**.

ul: Plants handled, strimming or gardening, walks through long vegetation, citrus drinks or cooking, perfumes.
Sun exposure in the previous 1–2 days; timing of symptoms.
Drugs (to exclude drug photosensitivity); previous similar episodes.
Shape and site of lesions; blister size and extent; eye involvement; signs of infection.
**Usually none.**
Swab if secondary infection is suspected.
Patch or photopatch testing only if allergic contact dermatitis is a possibility.
Biopsy rarely.

ddx.name: Allergic contact dermatitis (plants)
ddx.f: Very **itchy** eczema; needs sensitisation; does not need sun; spreads beyond the contact.

ddx.name: Drug photosensitivity
ddx.f: **Uniform** redness over all sun-exposed skin with a drug history (e.g. doxycycline, thiazides).

ddx.name: Sunburn
ddx.f: Uniform over exposed sites; no streaks.

ddx.name: Blister beetle dermatitis
ddx.f: Linear blisters after crushing a beetle; no sun needed.

ddx.name: Polymorphic light eruption
ddx.f: Itchy papules on sun-exposed skin hours after sun; recurrent each spring.

ddx.name: Non-accidental injury
ddx.f: Inconsistent or changing history, injuries in unusual places, other concerns: **safeguarding** assessment.

ddx.name: Burns or artefact
ddx.f: History of thermal or chemical injury; patterns may be self-inflicted.

ddx.name: Fixed drug eruption
ddx.f: Round dusky patches that recur at the same site with each dose.

ul: Treat the acute phase like a **superficial burn**; then protect the pigmented skin from the sun.
Explain the cause so the patient can avoid it; most cases settle without scarring.

blocks.h: Immediate care after contact (e.g. hogweed sap)

ul: **Wash off sap promptly with soap and water**, cover the skin and keep it **out of sunlight for at least 48 h**.
If sap gets in the eyes: rinse and seek **urgent eye assessment**.
Cool compresses, emollients and simple analgesia.
Leave blisters intact or use non-adherent dressings; keep clean (topical antiseptic only if needed).
**OTC hydrocortisone 1%** for mild small areas (not on broken skin).

drugs.name: Potent topical corticosteroid
drugs.dose: Short course of **5–7 days** to inflamed **intact** skin on the limbs or trunk; **moderate** potency on the face.
drugs.cautions: Not on broken or infected skin.
drugs.counsel: Apply thinly; stop when redness settles.

drugs.name: Secondary infection
drugs.use: Infected blisters: treat per NICE impetigo / secondary bacterial infection guidance.

ul: Reassure: it **fades slowly over months**.
**Strict sun protection** (even limited UV can darken it again): clothing, broad-spectrum high-SPF sunscreen.
Avoid bleaching agents unless advised by a specialist.
Learn to recognise **giant hogweed**; wear long sleeves, trousers and gloves when strimming or clearing plants.
Wash skin after gardening; avoid squeezing limes or applying citrus or perfume to skin before sun.

ladder.t: Wash off sap, 48 h out of sun, cool compresses, analgesia, emollient.
Potent topical steroid 5–7 days (moderate on face); antihistamine if itchy.
Reassurance and strict sun protection for months.
Large or blistering burns, face, genitals or hands: same-day urgent care or burns unit.

refer.t: Large or extensive blistering, burns on the **face, genitals or hands**, severe pain or infection: same-day GP, urgent care or **burns unit**.
Sap in the eye: urgent eye assessment.
**Safeguarding** concern in a child: follow local procedures.
Diagnostic doubt or persistent distressing pigmentation.

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

refer.t: Extensive hogweed burns, eye exposure, or blistering of the face, hands or genitals.
Unexplained marks in a child where the history does not fit: safeguarding.
Signs of infection: spreading redness, pus, fever.

ul: **Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation** for months, sometimes years.
Secondary bacterial infection of blisters.
Rarely scarring after severe bullous burns.
Misdiagnosis as abuse or burns causing distress.
The acute reaction settles in 1–2 weeks; pigment fades gradually over months with sun protection.
Recurs only with re-exposure.

pearls: Pigmentation, not the acute burn, is often why patients attend.
Tell gardeners about **giant hogweed**: sap plus sun is a classic UK summer presentation.
Ask about holidays, cocktails and cooking with limes.
Check for photosensitising drugs before blaming the plant.

Other light-related rashes: [polymorphic light eruption](condition:polymorphic-light-eruption), [drug-induced photosensitivity](condition:drug-photosensitivity) and [chronic actinic dermatitis](condition:chronic-actinic-dermatitis).

quiz.a: Plant furocoumarins (psoralens) on the skin plus UVA light.
No: it is phototoxic and needs no previous sensitisation.

quiz.q: When does it appear and peak?
quiz.a: About 24 h after exposure, peaking at 48–72 h.

quiz.q: What clue separates it from drug photosensitivity?
quiz.a: Bizarre streaks, drips and hand-prints that follow contact, not uniform sun-exposed redness.

quiz.q: Immediate advice after hogweed sap contact?
quiz.a: Wash with soap and water, cover and keep out of sunlight for at least 48 h.
Hand-prints and splashes in children can mimic non-accidental injury.
